primary_text_note: No local text under scripts/_retrofc/_texts/. Every quotation was checked against an online source: Gutenberg/anthology printings for the six pre-1920 poems, and Poetry Archive, LitCharts, Poem Analysis, WJEC/PMT board resources and school anthology PDFs for the nine in-copyright poems.

findings.claim: The plosive alliteration in “half” and the sibilance in “sunk” and “shattered” create a sense of violent destruction.
findings.truth: /h/ in “half” is a glottal fricative, not a plosive, and a single word cannot alliterate. Only the sibilance claim stands.
findings.evidence: Ozymandias l.4: ‘Half sunk a shattered visage lies’. Standard phonetic classification of /h/.

findings.claim: the “history” he was taught in British schools (Guy Fawkes, Dick Whittington, Lord Nelson)
findings.truth: Guy Fawkes is not named anywhere in ‘Checking Out Me History’. The British and nursery-rhyme figures Agard names are 1066, Dick Whittington, Lord Nelson and Waterloo, Columbus and 1492, Florence Nightingale, Robin Hood and ole King Cole.
findings.evidence: Full text, Poetry Archive: https://poetryarchive.org/poem/checking-out-me-history/ — no occurrence of Fawkes.

findings.claim: anaphora = “The use of words beginning with the same sound in close succession, creating emphasis or a particular effect.”
findings.truth: That is the definition of alliteration. Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or phrase at the start of successive lines or clauses — which is exactly what the surrounding sentence describes (Blake’s “In every” in stanza 2). The wrong definition sits in both the dfn data-def and the glossary entry.
findings.evidence: Blake, ‘London’ st.2: ‘In every cry of every Man, / In every Infant’s cry of fear, / In every voice, in every ban’.

findings.claim: the alternating structure (italicised British history vs bold Caribbean history)
findings.truth: Reversed, and “bold” is invented. In the AQA anthology the stanzas celebrating Toussaint, Nanny and Mary Seacole are printed in italics; the “Dem tell me” stanzas of British history are in plain roman type. Nothing in the poem is bold.
findings.evidence: AQA anthology printing; Poetry Archive and myedspace/Oak National notes both describe the italicised stanzas as the black-history sections.

findings.claim: “Toussaint / a slave / with a vision / lick back / Napoleon / battalion”
findings.truth: The poem reads ‘a slave / with vision’ — no article.
findings.evidence: Poetry Archive full text.

findings.claim: The present continuous “was running” creates immediacy.
findings.truth: “was running” is the past continuous.
findings.evidence: Hughes, ‘Bayonet Charge’ l.1: ‘Suddenly he awoke and was running – raw’.

findings.claim: Tennyson uses regular stanzas and a driving rhythm (repeated in flashcard 14: “Tennyson’s regular stanzas drive momentum”)
findings.truth: The six stanzas of ‘The Charge of the Light Brigade’ run 8, 9, 8, 12, 11 and 6 lines. The stanza lengths are irregular; what is regular is the dactylic metre and the repeated refrains.
findings.evidence: Tennyson, 1854 text, stanza lengths counted.

findings.claim: KC[2] “The poem is written in _____ couplets with iambic pentameter” keys “rhyming” as correct while offering “heroic” as a distractor.
findings.truth: A heroic couplet IS a rhyming couplet in iambic pentameter, so “heroic” is a second correct answer that the key marks wrong. The distractor has been replaced with “syllabic”.
findings.evidence: Standard definition of the heroic couplet; ‘My Last Duchess’ is routinely described as written in heroic couplets.

findings.claim: Wilfred Owen wrote ‘Exposure’ while serving in the trenches during the winter of 1917–18.
findings.truth: Owen was at Craiglockhart until November 1917 and then in Britain (Scarborough, then Ripon) for the whole of the winter of 1917–18; he did not return to France until August 1918. He drafted the poem at Scarborough in December 1917 and revised it until September 1918, drawing on the freezing weeks he had spent in the trenches in January–February 1917.
findings.evidence: Owen chronology (Britannica; Owen manuscript notes at the First World War Poetry Digital Archive / Oxford).

findings.claim: “The burying-party, picks and shovels in their shaking grasp”
findings.truth: The line reads ‘picks and shovels in shaking grasp’ — there is no “their”.
findings.evidence: Owen, ‘Exposure’, final stanza (poets.org; Poetry Lovers’ Page).

findings.claim: “the wizened earth has never troubled us / With hay”
findings.truth: Heaney writes ‘This wizened earth has never troubled us’.
findings.evidence: ‘Storm on the Island’ ll.3–4 (Death of a Naturalist, 1966).

findings.claim: the poem is also about the political turmoil of The Troubles / “Heaney uses nature as a metaphor for political fear during The Troubles”
findings.truth: ‘Storm on the Island’ was published in Death of a Naturalist in 1966, two years before the Troubles began — a date the lesson itself gives (c. 1968–1998) in its own glossary. The Stormont reading points to the sectarian tension already building, not to a conflict under way.
findings.evidence: Publication date 1966; the lesson’s own dfn dates the Troubles from c. 1968.

findings.claim: The compound noun “blood-shadow” and the image of the dead man “wandering” suggests the victim haunts the speaker.
findings.truth: “Wandering” appears nowhere in ‘Remains’. The poem reads ‘His blood-shadow stays on the street, and out on patrol / I walk right over it week after week.’ The fabricated quotation has been removed.
findings.evidence: Armitage, ‘Remains’, st.4 (The Not Dead, 2008).

findings.claim: the 2008 documentary film The Not Dead
findings.truth: The Not Dead (dir. Brian Hill) was broadcast on Channel 4 on 12 November 2007. The Pomona book of the poems followed in 2008.
findings.evidence: IMDb tt2060560; simonarmitage.com works page; Letterboxd (2007).

findings.claim: Duffy’s controlled quatrains reflect the photographer’s attempt to impose order on chaos.
findings.truth: ‘War Photographer’ is four six-line stanzas (sestets), not quatrains. The exam tip tells students to use this in the exam, so the wrong form label would be reproduced under AO2.
findings.evidence: Duffy, ‘War Photographer’ (Standing Female Nude, 1985): 4 x 6 lines, ABBCDD.

findings.claim: Form and structure — collapsing stanzas (Remains, breakdown) vs controlled quatrains (WP, imposed order)
findings.truth: Same error as F15: ‘War Photographer’ is four sestets. This sits inside the model exam plan students are told to copy.
findings.evidence: As F15.

findings.claim: “In his darkroom he is finally alone”
findings.truth: The printed text reads ‘In his dark room he is finally alone’ (two words).
findings.evidence: Anthology and WJEC resource printings of the poem.

findings.claim: “a shaven-headed full moon” — The metaphor compares the grandfather’s shaved head to the moon. (Repeated as flashcard 6: “Which metaphor describes the grandfather in Kamikaze?” → “A shaven-headed full moon.”)
findings.truth: Fabricated. There is no moon anywhere in ‘Kamikaze’ and no such line. The poem reads ‘a shaven head / full of powerful incantations’, and the shaven head is the pilot’s own, not the grandfather’s. A student reproducing this quotation would be quoting a poem that does not exist.
findings.evidence: Garland, ‘Kamikaze’ st.1 (The Invention of Fireworks, 2013): ‘with a flask of water, a samurai sword / in the cockpit, a shaven head / full of powerful incantations’.

findings.claim: His family “no longer spoke to him.”
findings.truth: Not in the poem. Garland writes ‘my mother never spoke again / in his presence, nor did she meet his eyes’. It is the mother, not “the family”, and the wording is different.
findings.evidence: ‘Kamikaze’, penultimate stanza.

findings.claim: indirect speech (“my mother / she said that”)
findings.truth: Not a line in the poem. The reporting phrases are ‘she thought, / recounting it later to her children’ and ‘And sometimes, she said, he must have wondered’.
findings.evidence: ‘Kamikaze’ st.2 and final stanza.

findings.claim: KC[2] “told through _____ speech” keys “indirect” while offering “reported” as a distractor.
findings.truth: “Reported speech” and “indirect speech” are synonyms, so the key marks a true answer wrong. The distractor has been replaced with “formal”.
findings.evidence: Standard grammatical terminology.

findings.claim: The poem is set on Armistice Day
findings.truth: ‘Poppies’ opens ‘Three days before Armistice Sunday and poppies had already been placed / on individual war graves.’ The setting is explicitly three days before, and Armistice Sunday, not Armistice Day.
findings.evidence: Weir, ‘Poppies’, l.1.

findings.claim: Mark scheme bullets: “‘Bleeding through their tissue paper white’ links the symbol to actual blood and violence” and “‘Tissue paper’ connects to fragility”.
findings.truth: Both quotations are fabricated. The words “tissue” and “bleeding” do not appear anywhere in ‘Poppies’. The poppy is ‘crimped petals, / spasms of paper red’. This is a mark scheme, so it teaches the invented quotation as the credit-worthy answer.
findings.evidence: Full text of ‘Poppies’ checked word by word (oatridge.co.uk; GradeSaver poem text).

findings.claim: Mark scheme bullet: “‘Trembling’ reveals what she is hiding.”
findings.truth: “Trembling” does not appear in ‘Poppies’. The mother ‘steeled the softening / of my face’ and ‘resisted the impulse’ — those are the lines that show suppressed emotion.
findings.evidence: As F23.

findings.claim: the “tissue paper” of the poppy represents both remembrance and the fragility of human life
findings.truth: “Tissue paper” is quoted as if from Weir but is not in her poem; the phrase belongs to the Dharker title being compared. Weir writes ‘spasms of paper red’.
findings.evidence: As F23.

findings.claim: “Maps too. The borderlines, the marks / that rivers make, roads, / railtracks, mountainfolds”
findings.truth: Dharker writes ‘Maps too. The sun shines through / their borderlines, the marks / that rivers make, roads, / railtracks, mountainfolds’. The quotation silently drops the light image that the lesson’s own argument depends on.
findings.evidence: ‘Tissue’, st.5 (school anthology PDFs; Poem Analysis).

findings.claim: Dharker references the “Koran” (Qur’an) as “the kind of paper / thinned by age or touching.”
findings.truth: The poem reads ‘Paper thinned by age or touching, / the kind you find in well-used books, / the back of the Koran’. The phrase “the kind of paper” is not in the poem.
findings.evidence: ‘Tissue’, st.1–2.

findings.claim: “a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary purpose, it upreared / Its head”, with “voluntary purpose” taught again in flashcards 7 and 8 and in the mark scheme.
findings.truth: Wordsworth writes ‘a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary power instinct, / Upreared its head.’ The word “purpose” comes from a different line eight lines later (‘with purpose of its own’). The misquotation is taught four times across the lesson.
findings.evidence: The Prelude (1850) Book I, boat-stealing episode — AQA anthology extract.

findings.claim: “One summer evening (led by her) / I found a little Boat tied to a Willow tree”
findings.truth: The AQA extract reads ‘One summer evening (led by her) I found / A little boat tied to a willow tree’. The line break falls after “I found”, and “boat” and “willow” are lower case throughout the extract (three further occurrences corrected for consistency).
findings.evidence: The Prelude (1850) Book I, opening of the AQA extract.

findings.claim: The boy returns the boat “with grave / And serious mood,”
findings.truth: The extract reads ‘and through the meadows homeward went, / In grave / And serious mood’ — “in”, not “with”.
findings.evidence: The Prelude (1850) Book I, close of the AQA extract.

findings.claim: Every lesson’s first mark scheme uses the label “Top band” twice: “Top band (26-30)… Upper band (21-25)… Top band (16-20)…”
findings.truth: 16–20 is not the top band; 26–30 is. A student reading the ladder is told 16 out of 30 is a top-band answer. The duplicate has been relabelled “Mid band (16-20)” in all ten lessons.
findings.evidence: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section B mark scheme: six levels of five marks, Level 6 = 26–30.

findings.claim: Lucrezia de’ Medici, died in suspicious circumstances in 1561 at the age of 17
findings.truth: Lucrezia di Cosimo de’ Medici was born 14 February 1545 and died 21 April 1561, so she was 16. Older reference works give her birth as c. 1544, which is where “17” comes from, so the figure is contested rather than plainly wrong. Not edited.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia and NCMA both give 1545–1561; Encyclopedia.com gives c. 1544–1561.

findings.claim: Practice question type labels across all ten lessons: “4 marks — Quote Analysis”, “8 marks — Extract Analysis”, and “30 marks — Poetry Comparison” on questions that name only one poem.
findings.truth: AQA Paper 2 Section B carries a single 30-mark comparative question and nothing else; there is no 4-mark or 8-mark question and no printed “extract” on this section (the named poem is printed in full). The labels are a house scaffold rather than board question types. Flagged for a unit-wide decision rather than edited, because the same labels run across the whole subject.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Paper 2 questions section: ‘Section B Poetry: students will answer one comparative question on one named poem printed on the paper and one other poem from their chosen anthology cluster.’

summary: Ten lessons checked; 33 findings (11 HIGH, 18 MEDIUM, 4 LOW), 31 of them fixed in 55 edits, 2 recorded as NOTE. The dominant failure mode is fabricated quotation: a non-existent 'shaven-headed full moon' taught as the key Kamikaze metaphor, 'Bleeding through their tissue paper white' and 'Trembling' invented for Poppies, 'wandering' invented for Remains, 'voluntary purpose' substituted for Wordsworth's 'voluntary power instinct' four times, and Guy Fawkes added to a poem that never mentions him. Also corrected: War Photographer called quatrains when it is four sestets (in both exam tips), Poppies set on Armistice Day when it opens three days before Armistice Sunday, Storm on the Island placed inside a conflict that began two years after publication, Owen placed in the trenches in a winter he spent in Yorkshire, anaphora defined as alliteration, two knowledge checks whose distractors were also correct answers, and a mark-scheme ladder that called 16-20 the top band in all ten lessons.
